title: The Undo Matrix: Which Command Undoes What
intro: Git has several 'undo' commands, and choosing the wrong one loses work. The right one depends on two questions: has the change been committed, and has it been pushed? This walks through each case.

steps.prompt: You edited src/cache.py and want to throw those uncommitted edits away entirely.
steps.fake_output: (no output: src/cache.py is back to its last committed state)
steps.why: This is the one undo with no safety net: uncommitted changes were never stored in Git, so no reflog can bring them back. If you might want them, 'git stash' instead.

steps.prompt: You committed too early. Undo the last commit but keep its changes staged, ready to recommit.
steps.fake_output: (no output: HEAD moved back one commit; the changes are staged)
steps.explanation: The commit is gone from the branch; its changes are in the index.
steps.why: The three reset modes differ only in how much they keep. --soft moves the branch and keeps everything staged; --mixed (the default) keeps the changes but unstages them; --hard discards them. All three move the branch pointer, so only use them on commits you haven't pushed.

steps.prompt: The last two commits were a dead end. Remove them and their changes completely.
steps.fake_output: HEAD is now at 3e1f0a9 Merge pull request #212
steps.explanation: The branch is two commits back and the working tree matches.
steps.why: The commits still exist in the object database, unreferenced, for about 30 days. 'git reflog' lists where HEAD has been, so 'git reset --hard HEAD@{1}' undoes this reset. That only works for committed work.

steps.prompt: A bad commit, b7c8d9e, is already on main and deployed. Undo its effect without rewriting shared history.
steps.fake_output:
[main 6f7a8b9] Revert "Switch to new pricing rules"
 3 files changed, 12 insertions(+), 48 deletions(-)
steps.explanation: A new commit that applies the exact opposite of b7c8d9e.
steps.why: Revert adds history instead of removing it, so nobody's clone breaks and there's a record of what happened. That's the rule: reset for private commits, revert for anything already shared.

steps.prompt: The bad change came in through a merge commit, 4d5e6f7. Revert the whole merge, keeping main's side (parent 1) as the mainline.
steps.fake_output:
[main 8a9b0c1] Revert "Merge pull request #230 from acme/feature/pricing"
 9 files changed, 31 insertions(+), 210 deletions(-)
steps.explanation: Everything the merge brought in has been undone on main.
steps.why: A merge commit has two parents, so Git needs to know which side to keep: -m 1 means 'the branch that was merged into'. One trap: Git still considers that branch merged, so merging it again later brings nothing back. You must revert the revert first (git-incident-006).

steps.prompt: You just ran a rebase and it made a mess. Put the branch back exactly where it was before the rebase.
steps.fake_output: HEAD is now at 9f2c1e7 Add audit log table
steps.explanation: The branch points at its pre-rebase commit again.
steps.why: Git saves the previous position in ORIG_HEAD before dangerous operations (rebase, merge, reset). It's the quickest undo for 'that last big command was a mistake'; the reflog is the fuller history when ORIG_HEAD has already been overwritten.
